new_statements.quote: El quechua posee una forma cag que puede traducirse como ‘eso que es’. [...] su uso común con ciertas palabras como ali ‘bueno’ lo ha convertido en una forma ligada. nogapag cag ‘lo que es para mí’ (partícula libre) / alicag ‘el que es bueno, el bueno’ (partícula ligada). Se puede saber que en el segundo caso la partícula es ligada por la colocación de la fuerza de la voz que en quechua recae en la penúltima sílaba: a.'li.cag NO 'a.li # cag [p.50: Cabe anotar que los datos (vea el apéndice) corresponden principalmente a las variedades que se hablan en el departamento de Huánuco, especialmente las variedades de Ambo-Pasco, Margos-Yarowilca-Lauricocha (MYL) y Huamalíes.]
new_statements.translation: Quechua has a form cag 'that which is' ... its common use with certain words such as ali 'good' has turned it into a bound form: nogapag cag 'what is for me' (free particle) / alicag 'the one that is good' (bound particle). One can tell that in the second case the particle is bound from the placement of stress ('the force of the voice'), which in Quechua falls on the penultimate syllable: a.'li.cag, NOT 'a.li # cag. [p.50: The data correspond principally to the varieties spoken in the department of Huánuco, especially Ambo-Pasco, Margos-Yarowilca-Lauricocha and Huamalíes.]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the (phonological) word; a clitic/suffix that becomes bound counts toward the word, shifting stress rightward (a.'li.cag vs. 'a.li + cag).
new_statements.exceptions: None in Toliver's chapter. The companion chapter in the same volume (Weber & Landerman 2008: 25-26) notes for central Quechua generally that a word-final long vowel (e.g. 1st-person -V:) attracts stress to the final syllable, and that Huallaga also stresses other final long vowels; not stated specifically for Ambo-Pasco.
new_statements.domain_note: Word domain incl. bound particles/enclitics (the example uses stress placement as a diagnostic of boundness). Passing remark in a loan-phonology article, phrased for 'quechua' in general by the Ambo-Pasco field linguist; data principally Ambo-Pasco (p.50).
new_statements.identity_note: Toliver's 2008 loanword/nickname article states (p.50) that its data 'corresponden principalmente a las variedades que se hablan en el departamento de Huánuco, especialmente las variedades de Ambo-Pasco, Margos-Yarowilca-Lauricocha (MYL) y Huamalíes'; the stress remark on p.52 is phrased for 'quechua' generally and the example a.'li.cag is in Ambo-Pasco orthography (g = voiced postvelar). Toliver is the SIL field linguist for Ambo-Pasco [qva] (provinces of Ambo, Huánuco and Pasco, Pasco). No dedicated phonology of ambo1252 was found; the statement is a passing first-hand remark, not a stress section.

sources.note: p.52: stress ('la fuerza de la voz') in Quechua falls on the penultimate syllable, shown by a.'li.cag (bound cag) vs *'a.li # cag; data principally Ambo-Pasco, MYL and Huamalíes (p.50). Section 4 treats syllable structure and segment adaptation of Spanish loans, no further stress rule.

sources.citation: Weber, David & Peter Landerman. 2008. La interpretación de las vocales largas en el quechua. In Coombs & Bergli (eds.), Estudios quechuas II (SLP 55), 12-28. Lima: ILV.

sources.note: pp.25-26: 'En la mayoría de las variedades centrales del quechua, el acento se asigna a la penúltima sílaba'; word-final long vowel (1st person) is stressed; Huallaga also stresses other final long vowels; some Ancash varieties initial stress with phrase-final heavy-syllable stress (Parker 1976). General central-Quechua, not Pasco-specific.
